meta.title: Who really said "We cannot cure the world of sorrows, but we can choose to live in joy"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Joseph Campbell really said it — but not in The Hero with a Thousand Faces. Quote Investigator traces the line to the 1991 companion edited by Diane K. Osbon.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We cannot cure the world of sorrows, but we can choose to live in joy'?
meta.ogDescription: Campbell said it — but not in The Hero with a Thousand Faces. The line comes from the 1991 companion edited by Diane K. Osbon.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1904–1987 · American writer & scholar of comparative mythology
answer.sourceLine: The line appears in Reflections on the Art of Living: A Joseph Campbell Companion (HarperCollins, 1991), selected and edited by Diane K. Osbon — a book assembled after Campbell’s death. Quote Investigator ↗ verified it against a hardcopy in the chapter “In the Field,” where Osbon says she recorded these words directly from Campbell over years in his company.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Reflections on the Art of Living: A Joseph Campbell Companion
Chapter “In the Field” — quote pages 8 and 17
Diane K. Osbon, from journals kept over years in Campbell’s company

source.excerpt: We cannot cure the world of sorrows, but we can choose to live in joy. When we talk about settling the world’s problems, we’re barking up the wrong tree. The world is perfect. It’s a mess. It has always been a mess. We are not going to change it. Our job is to straighten out our own lives.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ locates the wording in the 1991 book Reflections on the Art of Living: A Joseph Campbell Companion, chapter “In the Field,” pages 8 and 17, marked “verified with hardcopy,” and concludes Campbell should receive credit on the testimony of editor Diane K. Osbon.

The Internet Archive holds the 1991 HarperCollins edition ↗ — Joseph Campbell as author, Diane K. Osbon as editor — catalogued with the title elements reversed, as A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living. Both orderings refer to the same book.

The Joseph Campbell Foundation ↗, which publishes the book today, describes the material as drawn from a month-long workshop at the Esalen Institute held in celebration of Campbell’s eightieth birthday.

Wikiquote’s Campbell page ↗ cites this same 1991 companion by page number for three other sayings, and has a dedicated section for The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) — yet this line appears in neither. A correct attribution with no page number is exactly the gap that lets the wrong book take hold.
source.excerptNote: As reproduced by Quote Investigator ↗ from a hardcopy. QI’s citation covers pages 8 and 17, so even this block is gathered from two places in the chapter rather than one unbroken paragraph — the book sets these sayings out as short standalone lines.

author.name: Joseph Campbell
author.heading: Who was Joseph Campbell?
author.metaLine: 1904–1987 · American writer & scholar of comparative mythology
author.bio: Joseph Campbell taught literature at Sarah Lawrence College and spent a career in comparative mythology and comparative religion, arguing that the world’s myths are variations on one human story — the case he made in The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) and that reached a mass audience through his PBS conversations with Bill Moyers, The Power of Myth. He died in October 1987. A great deal of what circulates as “Campbell” today, this line included, comes from books built after his death out of lectures, workshops, and the notebooks of people who sat with him.

misattribution.heading: What travels wrong
misattribution.intro: The name on this one is right. What goes wrong is the book it gets pinned to, and the way three separate Campbell lines get welded into a single paragraph.

items.why: Goodreads files the passage under Campbell’s 1949 monograph ↗, and the credit spreads from there. Quote Investigator ↗ found the wording in the 1991 Osbon companion instead — a compilation of remarks recorded in conversation. Wikiquote’s Campbell page ↗, which quotes both books, carries the line in neither.

It usually circulates as one continuous quotation opening “Participate joyfully in the sorrows of the world” and closing with a line about the warrior’s approach. Those are separate sayings: the Joseph Campbell Foundation ↗ gives the joyful-participation line as “Joyfully participate in the sorrows of the world and everything changes,” sourced to Sukhavati, not to the 1991 companion.

PassItOn runs the line with nothing but ‘Joseph Campbell, lecturer and writer’ ↗ — no book, no date, no page. A correct name with no source is how a quote ends up attached to the wrong book a few reposts later.

misattribution.truthLine: The documented record is a single sentence in the chapter “In the Field” of the 1991 companion, taken from Diane K. Osbon’s journals of her time with Campbell — verified against a hardcopy by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: It reads like a fridge magnet, and by now it is one — but the sentence was never meant to stand alone. In the book it is the opening of a short run of lines that get much blunter: the world is a mess, it has always been a mess, we are not going to change it, and the job in front of you is your own life.

That continuation is the part the internet drops, and dropping it flips the meaning. Quoted alone, the line can read as permission to look away. With the next four lines attached, it reads as an argument about where to put your effort — closer to a warning against grand fixes than to a case for cheerfulness.
detailsBody: Campbell did not write this book. The Joseph Campbell Foundation ↗ describes it as drawn from a month-long workshop at the Esalen Institute held to celebrate his eightieth birthday, and Quote Investigator ↗ quotes Osbon describing the chapter this line sits in as “favorite expressions of his, recorded in my journals over the years in his company.” So the wording is Campbell’s speech as caught by his editor, not a sentence he drafted and published.

Quote Investigator sets one parallel beside it: Kurt Vonnegut’s A Man Without a Country (2005) makes a similar point about the planet always having been a mess. QI presents that as a resemblance, not a rival origin — it does not suggest Vonnegut wrote Campbell’s line.
context.pull: The world is perfect. It’s a mess.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator credits Joseph Campbell on Diane K. Osbon's testimony and cites the 1991 book Reflections on the Art of Living: A Joseph Campbell Companion, chapter 'In the Field', quote pages 8 and 17, HarperCollins, verified with hardcopy; it also notes Kurt Vonnegut made a similar point in A Man Without a Country (2005).

The Internet Archive holds the 1991 HarperCollins edition of the book, credited to Joseph Campbell with Diane K. Osbon as editor, catalogued as 'A Joseph Campbell companion : reflections on the art of living', borrowable/access-restricted.

The Joseph Campbell Foundation sells the book and describes the material as 'Drawn from a month-long workshop at the world-famous Esalen Institute held in celebration of the scholar's eightieth birthday.'

The Joseph Campbell Foundation gives the related line as 'Joyfully participate in the sorrows of the world and everything changes,' attributed to Sukhavati: Place of Bliss, and does not quote 'We cannot cure the world of sorrows.'

Wikiquote's Joseph Campbell page cites 'A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living' (1991) at pages 18, 19 and 152 for other quotations, has a section for The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949), and contains no instance of 'cure the world of sorrows', 'live in joy' or 'Participate joyfully'. It gives his dates as 26 March 1904 – 30 October 1987.

Goodreads displays the merged passage ('Participate joyfully in the sorrows of the world. We cannot cure the world of sorrows, but we can choose to live in joy. The warrior's approach...') and attributes it to The Hero with a Thousand Faces.
PassItOn reproduces 'We cannot cure the world of sorrows, but we can choose to live in joy.' credited only to 'Joseph Campbell, lecturer and writer', with no book, date or citation.

Wikipedia gives Joseph Campbell's dates as March 26, 1904 – October 30, 1987, describes him as an American writer and professor of literature at Sarah Lawrence College working in comparative mythology and comparative religion, and lists A Joseph Campbell Companion (1991) among works published posthumously.
